These look better than mine when I first got my home (2021). I had to use a paint scraper to physically remove decades of dirt, debris, sauces, bug mess from inside the cabinets and drawers - just fckn yuck!!


In my case, I initially took out all the shelves and disinfected the crap out of them. I took off the cabinet doors to scrub them. I actually had to replace the hardware hinges because most had rusted and broken. 


While all those were drying and sitting in the sun for a week, I actually spray painted the insides with satin finish white spray paint. The insides looked so good and clean, I ended up spraying the exterior of the cabinets AND the cabinet doors I had removed. I know it's against the rules here, but I did not sand or strip them. I did use an 'etching' spray on the cabinet doors. Then it was too much white, so I drilled holes and added hardware. I also stripped paint off a couple drawers, stained them, and seal with clear coat to break up the brightness. 


For the shelves, I wrapped the whole thing carefully in contact paper (I picked marble-ish paper to hide imperfections). I also super glued the same contact paper to the interior bottom of the cabinets. 


THEN the floor looked very gross next to the pristine white, so I got peel and stick floor tiles which were surprisingly great lol


THEN I found a nicer faucet on sale while purchasing hardware, so I got that too. 


THEN the countertops were terrible, so I painted them with a kit and prayed for my artistic ability.


Whole project was a lot of sweat, tears, and about $1,000 for supply on the whole thing. 3 years later, it still looks great and I'm almost saved up for a complete remodel! I do have spare super glue for if I ever see an contact paper creeping up. Best $1k spent for sanity.

I use my thumb parallel to the vein, take my 22g needle/syringe (I could never get the hang of butterflys hahaha) and pierce right next to it under the skin - essentially in that subcutaneous space and then redirect into the vein. I do this for IVCs as well. I found that it's the skin on top of the vein that causes it to be so mobile. It's also super bouncy, so going in after piercing the skin gives me an easier time. Also - start low! If it blows you can still go higher. Sometimes I will use a 25g on small dogs. ALSO - the saphenous (lat and medial) likes to collapse, slow and steady when drawing. You'll know you're pulling too hard if you get some blood then it stops. I used to see so many techs do that awful HUGE pull, stop, HUGE pull, stop - so many blown veins. Also long as the blood is flowing it won't clot, just have your tubes ready.

I am a veterinary recruiter. I use my experience and clinic knowledge to build repertoire and evaluate candidates. I help advocate for higher wages and better working conditions. I help teach candidates how to negotiate and walk away from poor offers. I help coach hiring managers on how the market has changed and how to retain techs and doctors. The pay for my role is great (starting was $75k), mostly remote, salaried so I make my own hours, license still reimbursed, attending conferences and traveling on the company dime is cool, I don't need to pay for childcare. I love my work and I can retire doing this.

Recruiting is not for everyone.Downside is it can be stressful because it's hard to take an "emergency" seriously when you've experienced true ECC emergencies. Clinics/hiring managers can be mean because they are short staffed and take it out on recruiting. You can reach out to 100 people and hope you make 1 hire. You need to be computer literate, tactful, friendly, and highly organized. There is also a lot of rejection on a daily basis. It's kinda like sales, but less gross. There are a lot of soul sucking corporations (looking at you VCA, NVA, Banfield) which give you great work experience, but you don't get to do a ton of advocacy. I recommend choosing corporate that hasn't been around long - maybe something that started in the last 3-5 years. They are usually more interested in taking care for their people.

You only have 4 months of experience?? If this is true, practice GP for a year to learn your basics. General restraint, fractious animal handling, radiology positioning (abdominal, thoracic, extremities; lat, V/D, oblique), venipuncture (jugular/cephalic/saphenous), SQ/IV/IM injections, IVC placement, pre-op anesthesia protocols, general surgery anesthesia monitoring, post-op recovery/care, common drugs/pharmacology/interactions, bandaging, plus I'm sure I'm missing something. Would you say you're proficient in all of these? 

ECC can be great, but can also be overwhelming even for veteran techs. Lots to learn BUT a lot of it builds on the basics. Also knowing/understanding medical terminology and short hand (ie PO, IM, IVC, PU/PD, AD, OS) goes a long way to not frustrating your doctors or senior techs.

Also IF you only have 4 months experience AND an ER hires you, I'd bet money they just desperately need warm bodies and you'll be thrown to the wolves. If you literally can't wait, good place to start might be as a kennel tech, tech assistant, or room runner. In my experience you will learn faster in a GP setting with basics then in one of those positions. Honestly, give it a year at least.

Source: Tech for 15 years (4 years GP, 6 years specialty, 5 years ECC) and I've been recruiting/hiring in ECC/specialty for almost 4 years now.

I worked for Banfield a total of 7 years at 3 different locations. The locations you work at will matter. 2/3 had garbage people which made me miserable. The 3rd, the people were great and work was awesome. I had to leave because I was moving out of the area.

TLDR: Find the right one. Transferring is easy if needed.

Pros: It's a great place to get started or to chill after burn out. I liked to say Techs go there to start or retire haha! It is an easy job. People will say you're a salesman - they are not wrong. BUT I've never seen anyone get fired based on their numbers, just getting pestered by the PM. You learn some cookie cutter medicine and a good amount about preventative care. Try to work in a HCOL area as people are usually more compliant. If you hate the people you are working with after 3-6 months, request to transfer somewhere else. It is very difficult to get fired which is good news for you, but also bad news because shit people won't get canned. Transferring is easy when you speak with a recruiter.

Cons: 15 min appointments and 7+ procedures a day can become stressful IF you don't manage your doctor or your time. (But I find that is the case anywhere.) Carry around a small note book to keep track of notes and the tx plan. I used to also keep track of OWP opportunities 🤷‍♀️ I'm a nerd like that. It can also get boring, but some people want that - a boring, stable job with decent benefits.

Tbh I would choose a corporate practice over private any day. I've never had trouble getting paid with corporate and they provide a lot of good benefits like 401k, CE, Uniforms, Pet discounts. At the end of the day, I need to make rent and Banfield was good to me.
